clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive complicated hereditary spastic paraplegia caused by biallelic loss of maspardin, encoded by SPG21 (ACP33)
Classically described in the Old Order Amish, in whom a founder frameshift variant is responsible
Onset is usually in early adulthood with slowly progressive spastic paraparesis followed by cognitive decline and dementia
Additional features include cerebellar and extrapyramidal signs, dysarthria and sometimes psychiatric disturbance
Neuroimaging characteristically shows a thin corpus callosum and periventricular white-matter change
Maspardin is thought to regulate endosomal trafficking and receptor recycling, linking SPG21 to other trafficking-related complicated HSPs
Management is symptomatic and supportive, with physiotherapy, spasticity control and cognitive and psychiatric support
reference.pathophysiology: MAST syndrome (SPG21) is caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in the gene encoding maspardin, a protein associated with endosomal and trans-Golgi membranes that appears to regulate intracellular trafficking and receptor recycling, including modulation of CD4-related signalling. Loss of maspardin is thought to disturb endosomal sorting and membrane homeostasis in neurons, leading to a diffuse neurodegenerative process. This affects the corticospinal tracts, cerebral white matter (with the characteristic thin corpus callosum), cerebellum and basal ganglia, producing the combination of spastic paraparesis, dementia and mixed cerebellar and extrapyramidal features that defines the syndrome.
additionalDifferentials: SPG11 and SPG15 complicated hereditary spastic paraplegia with thin corpus callosum
Other autosomal recessive hereditary spastic paraplegias
Wilson disease and other treatable movement-disorder mimics
additionalInvestigations: SPG21 sequencing within a hereditary spastic paraplegia or complicated-HSP panel
MRI of brain showing thin corpus callosum and white-matter change
Neuropsychological assessment to characterise cognitive decline
Nerve conduction studies to identify any peripheral involvement
Metabolic screen and copper studies to exclude treatable mimics
Family history and consanguinity assessment supporting recessive inheritance
redFlags: Rapidly progressive cognitive decline requiring exclusion of treatable dementias
New extrapyramidal signs suggesting an alternative or coexisting movement disorder
Acute behavioural or psychiatric deterioration needing urgent support
Loss of safe swallowing or mobility indicating advancing disease
reference.prognosis: MAST syndrome progresses slowly but is a multisystem neurodegenerative disorder, and over years affected individuals develop increasing motor disability and dementia with substantial dependence.
pitfalls: Overlooking the diagnosis outside the Amish population, where it is rarer and less expected
Attributing early spastic gait to a pure HSP and missing evolving cognitive decline
Failing to recognise thin corpus callosum as a clue to a complicated recessive HSP
Neglecting psychiatric and cognitive needs while focusing only on spasticity
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: No disease-modifying therapy; management is supportive with regular physiotherapy to maintain mobility and prevent contractures in the spastic paraparesis
Antispasticity treatment with agents such as baclofen or tizanidine, and focal botulinum toxin injection for troublesome spasticity
Mobility aids, orthoses and occupational therapy as disability progresses
Cognitive assessment and dementia support, with management of psychiatric and behavioural disturbance
Speech and language therapy for dysarthria and swallowing safety
Autosomal recessive with founder variants: offer genetic counselling and family screening, addressing consanguinity
Coordinate care through a neurology-led multidisciplinary team
